resources.string: Root access check
Verifies superuser access; triggers your root manager\'s grant prompt

This check runs the `id` command as root. It is the moment your root manager (Magisk, KernelSU, APatch) shows its grant prompt. The check cannot be turned off because it is the consent mechanism itself: without it, no other entry can ask for root.
Force-stop target app
Kills the selected app\'s process, like Android\'s \"Force stop\". Unsaved in-app state is lost.

Runs `am force-stop` on the selected target. This kills the process; it does not relaunch it — relaunching is a separate entry. Only packages in the module\'s 45-app Xposed scope (plus `com.whatsapp` and `com.whatsapp.w4b`) are accepted; the module\'s own package is rejected. When disabled, WAEX falls back to a signed-broadcast restart that cannot verify the process actually died.
Relaunch target app
Opens the selected app

Runs Android\'s `monkey` launcher command against the selected target. Acceptance is verified by parsing the `Events injected: N` line — a missing line means launch failed and WAEX falls back to a standard launcher intent. Same scope validation as the force-stop entry.
Create staging file
Creates an empty staging file in /data/local/tmp, used only for this install and deleted afterwards

Runs `mktemp /data/local/tmp/waex.XXXXXX`. The returned path must match a strict regex (`^/data/local/tmp/waex\\.[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) before any later step may use it; an attacker-planted path is rejected. The file is owned by root and is deleted in the `finally` block of the install flow.
Stage update file
Copies the verified update APK from WAEX\'s cache into the staging file and confirms the byte count matches

Copies the downloaded APK from the app cache into the staging path returned by `mktemp`, then runs `wc -c` to confirm the byte count equals the source APK size. A size mismatch aborts the install before `pm install` runs. The staging path is treated as a `DERIVED_OUTPUT` — it can only come from the `mktemp` step\'s policy-passing output.
Install WAEX update
Installs the downloaded WAEX update, replacing the version currently installed. WAEX closes itself to finish.

Runs `pm install -r -d --user 0` on the staging file. `-r` replaces the existing install; `-d` also permits installing a lower versionCode (only used when you select an older release from the GitHub releases list). On success, WAEX kills its own process to finish the swap. On failure, the staging file is still cleaned up. The 70-second timeout survives an interactive root-manager prompt on slow devices.
Remove staging file
Deletes the temporary staging file
Runs `rm -f --` on the staging path in the install flow\'s `finally` block, whether the install succeeded or failed. Best-effort: a cleanup failure does not roll back a successful install.
Check running processes
Reports whether each WhatsApp app is currently running (process IDs only)

Runs a multi-line `pidof` script — one `pidof` call per scoped package — and emits a `PID|<package>|<pids>` line per target. A trailing `END|WAEX_PROCESS_SNAPSHOT` sentinel authenticates the output; truncated or polluted output is discarded. A running process is not proof of hook initialization — only that the process exists.
SELinux status
Reads the device\'s SELinux mode (Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled)

Runs `getenforce` as the third fallback after the `/sys/fs/selinux/enforce` read and the `android.os.SELinux` reflection path fail. Never triggers a fresh superuser request: this entry only runs when root has already been granted. Output is validated against the three canonical values.
Detect HMA (Zygisk)
Looks inside /data/adb/modules for a Hide My Applist Zygisk module and whether it is enabled

Checks the canonical Zygisk module path (`/data/adb/modules/hma_oss_zygisk`) and lists any other module directory whose name contains `hma`. An enabled module is reported as `active`. The probe is read-only.
Detect HMA (LSPosed)
Copies LSPosed\'s module database to WAEX\'s cache, checks whether HMA is enabled in it, then deletes the copy

Copies `/data/adb/lspd/config/modules_config.db` (plus its `-wal` and `-shm` siblings) into WAEX\'s cache directory, queries the local copy for an enabled HMA row, then deletes the copy. The cache copy is briefly world-readable (`chmod 666`) for the local SQLite read — this is why the entry is rated LOW, not INFO: the copied DB exposes the enabled-module list even though only HMA rows are queried.
Copy LSPosed DB to cache
Copies LSPosed\'s module database and its -wal/-shm siblings into WAEX\'s cache so a local SQLite read can check for HMA

Runs `cp` on `modules_config.db` plus its `-wal` and `-shm` siblings into WAEX\'s cache directory, then `chmod 666` on the copies so the local SQLite open succeeds. The copies are deleted by the caller after the read. Briefly world-readable — this is the LOW-risk part of the LSPosed probe split out for audit transparency.
List HMA-like packages
Requests the full list of installed apps from the system, keeps only names that look like HMA variants

Runs `pm list packages` and locally filters the result for package names whose lowercased form contains `hma`, `hidemyapp`, or ends with `.hmal`. Used both as a discovery probe and as the target list for the `hma.force_stop` entry.
Locate HMA configs
Searches five system data folders for HMA\'s config.json files and collects their paths (read-only)

Runs `find` across `/data/misc`, `/data/system`, `/data/adb`, `/data/user/0` and `/data/data` for `config.json` files under paths matching `*hma*` or `*hide_my_applist*`. Hardening rider: `-type f -xdev -maxdepth 8`, symlinks and unusual files are ignored, the first 20 hits are processed and any overflow is counted, the sweep has its own 8-second budget. Discovery has no side effects: sweep output feeds only `hma.read_config` and the UI.
Read HMA config
Reads the contents of a discovered HMA configuration file

Runs `head -c 262144` on a discovered path. The path parameter must pass the strict-path check (`^/data/[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$`, no `..`, no shell metacharacters, no whitespace) — discovered paths that fail it are refused. This is the R1 fix from the privilege analysis: an attacker-planted path like `hma$(touch /data/local/tmp/pwned)/config.json` fails validation before any shell sees it. Read is capped at 256 KiB; real HMA configs are tens of KB.
Back up HMA config
Saves a backup copy of the HMA config before any change is made

Runs `cp -p <config> <config>.waex.bak` followed by `restorecon`. A `WAEX_HMA_BACKUP_OK` sentinel must be present in the output; a missing sentinel causes the entire config to be skipped — the write step refuses to run unless the backup succeeded.
Apply HMA fix
Rewrites HMA\'s configuration file in place, removing the rules that hide or block WAEX. Owner and permissions are preserved; a backup is created first.

Atomically rewrites the HMA config: `stat` the owner, `base64 -d` into a `.tmp` file, `chown`, `chmod 600`, `restorecon`, `mv -f` over the live config, then re-`chown`/`chmod`/`restorecon`. A `WAEX_HMA_WRITE_OK` sentinel authenticates the write; the config is then re-read and re-parsed to confirm the WAEX-hiding rules are gone. If verification fails, the backup is automatically restored. The 8-second budget (raised from 4s to halve the kill-window on slow storage) is what closes the R9 mid-write race.
Restore HMA backup
Copies the pre-edit backup back over the HMA config — only when the written config fails verification

Runs `cp -p <config>.waex.bak <config>` followed by `restorecon`. This step is automatic on the failure path of `hma.write_config`; it is not a user-facing \"restore\" button. A manual undo would be a separate registry entry with its own trigger.
Stop HMA apps
Force-stops installed HMA apps before and after the config edit so they can\'t overwrite it. Apps are matched by package-name pattern.

Runs `am force-stop` on every installed package whose name passes the HMA pattern check (well-formed package name containing `hma`, `hidemyapp`, or ending in `.hmal`). Runs both before and after the config edit so a running HMA process cannot overwrite the fix. Honest residual: apps merely named like HMA also get stopped — the registry narrows matching to well-formed names, but cannot eliminate incidental matches.

Test echo
Echoes text through the registry pipeline for testing

Debug-build-only entry. Base64-encodes arbitrary text on the client and runs `echo <base64> | base64 -d` as root to exercise the full runner → gate → validate → template → exec → output-policy → audit pipeline without touching a real operation.
